opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, what surprised me most was how emotional people's reactions were. Inside the field, we tend to look at a release through a technical lens: what's the success rate on held-out tasks, how well does it generalize to new objects, how much embodiment transfer are we seeing. But when the videos went out, the responses from people outside AI were much more visceral.

Some of it was delight. People would watch the robot fold an origami fox or pack a lunch bag and say, "I didn't know robots could do that yet." There's a gap between where the research frontier actually is and where the public assumes it is, and a lot of folks were still picturing the stiff, pre-programmed arms you see in car factories. Seeing a robot respond to a casual spoken instruction and adapt when someone moves the object around shifted their mental model.

But there was also a real undercurrent of anxiety. A lot of comments were along the lines of, "Okay, so what happens to my job?" or "Should I be worried about this in my home?" With language models, people had a couple of years to get used to the idea of AI that talks. Physical AI feels different. It's in the room with you, it can touch things, and that makes the stakes feel more concrete. I think that's a very reasonable reaction, and it's one reason we put so much emphasis on safety, both the semantic side, like understanding whether an action is appropriate, and the physical side, like collision avoidance and force limits.

The third thing that struck me was how many people assumed the videos were teleoperated or sped up. That skepticism is healthy, honestly. The field has a history of very polished demos that don't hold up, so I understand why people are cautious. It pushed us to be more transparent about what's autonomous, what the failure modes are, and where the system still struggles. Because it does still struggle. Dexterity is hard, long-horizon tasks are hard, and robustness in truly messy, unstructured homes is still an open problem.

So overall, the public reaction reminded me that robotics isn't just a research problem. It's a social one. How these systems get introduced, how honest we are about their limits, and how we bring people along matter just as much as the benchmarks.

r001.rationale: The response describes emotional reactions to the robot demos and contrasts public reactions with technical evaluation, but it does not say viewers focused more on the robot’s humanlike form than on the VLM/VLA work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that struck me most was how much people were reacting to the mundane stuff rather than the flashy stuff. Inside the team, we'd spent months obsessing over the hard technical pieces, like long-horizon reasoning, how the model generalizes to objects and instructions it's never seen, how it handles the embodiment gap across different robot platforms. And then the release goes out and the clips that go viral are the robot folding a piece of paper, or putting glasses into a case, or packing a lunch box. Things that are deeply unremarkable if a person does them.

And I think that's actually the right reaction, in a way. People who don't work in robotics have a very reasonable mental model where the physical world is easy and chess is hard, because that's how it feels from the inside as a human. So when they see a robot do something a toddler can do, and it's actually a big deal, there's this moment of recalibration. A lot of the messages I got were basically some version of "wait, this was the hard part?" And yes, this was the hard part. Moravec's paradox is real and it's still with us.

The second thing I noticed was the emotional range. The reactions split pretty cleanly into wonder and anxiety, and often from the same person within the same message. Someone would say "this is incredible" and then two sentences later ask whether their job was going to exist in five years. I don't think we in the research community always appreciate how quickly a demo translates into a personal question for someone watching it. For us it's a benchmark. For them it's "what does this mean for my kitchen, my warehouse, my parents' care."

And then there was a kind of skepticism that I actually found healthy. People asking how cherry-picked the clips were, how many takes, whether it was teleoperated. Those are exactly the questions I'd want someone to ask, and I think the field has earned that skepticism over the years with a lot of very polished demo videos. So I tried to engage with that honestly rather than get defensive about it. The gap between a good demo and a robot you'd actually leave alone in your house is still enormous, and I'd rather people understand that than be over-impressed.

r001.rationale: The response says viewers focused on mundane tasks rather than the technical challenges, but it does not say they noticed the robot’s humanlike form more readily than the underlying VLM and VLA work.

astra-6.text:
What struck me was how differently people interpreted the same demonstration. Within the AI community, people tend to ask about generalization: what’s new here, what did the robot see during training, and what can it do in an unfamiliar situation? Outside that community, the questions become much more immediate: could this help me at home? Could it take over a task I find tedious or difficult?

And that’s a useful shift in perspective. We spend so much time thinking about the technical challenges that it’s easy to lose sight of what makes robotics meaningful to people. They’re imagining how it might fit into their lives. At the same time, a demonstration can make the technology feel closer to being ready for everyday use than it actually is, so communicating the limitations is just as important as showing the capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts technical questions from AI insiders with practical questions from outsiders, but it does not say outsiders noticed the robot’s humanlike form more readily than the VLM and VLA work.

sol-6.1.text:
What struck me was how differently people reacted depending on their background. Within the AI community, people were interested in the model—how it generalized, how it followed instructions, what was new technically. Outside that community, the questions were much more immediate: “Can this help me at home? Could it help my parents? When can I actually use it?”

It’s a useful reminder that people don’t experience robotics as a benchmark. They see a robot doing something in the physical world, and they connect it to their own lives. And then you have to explain the gap between a compelling demonstration and something that’s reliable enough to be useful every day.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts technical questions from the AI community with practical questions from others, but it does not say that outside viewers noticed the robot’s humanlike form more readily than the underlying VLM and VLA work.
